bib.title: Fine-Grained Human Feedback Gives Better Rewards for Language Model Training
bib.venue: NeurIPS 2023 (37th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems)

read.skipped: Reference list skimmed; figure images (annotation interface, Fig 5-8) not visible in text

question: Can fine-grained human feedback (dense, per-error-type rewards) give better RL training signals for language models than holistic preference rewards?
hypothesis: Dense rewards localised to segments, from separate reward models per error type, are a stronger and more sample-efficient training signal than a single sequence-level reward.
contributions: FINE-GRAINED RLHF framework with rewards dense in segment density and multiple reward models per feedback type
QA-FEEDBACK dataset with fine-grained and preference human feedback
Experiments on detoxification and long-form QA with automatic and human evaluation, plus LM customization via reward weights
Release of data, feedback and code

method.summary: PPO is run with a reward that sums K reward models, each scoring segments at its own density (sub-sentence, sentence, full sequence) with weights w_k plus a per-token KL penalty. Evaluated on detoxification (Perspective API reward, GPT-2 large) and long-form QA (T5-large with three Longformer-base reward models trained on span-level human feedback).
method.task: detoxification (REALTOXICITYPROMPTS) and long-form QA (QA-FEEDBACK, built from ASQA)

datasets.name: QA-FEEDBACK (from ASQA)
datasets.split: train and dev from ASQA train; test from ASQA dev; 1K train examples used for SFT, feedback collected on remaining 2,853 train and 500 dev outputs
datasets.source: ASQA with oracle knowledge contexts; passages mapped by BM25 to closest passage; fine-grained and preference feedback from 15 selected Amazon Mechanical Turk workers; released at FineGrainedRLHF.github.io
datasets.preprocessing: Spans of C1 errors shorter than 5 words filtered for Rphi1 training; sentences via spaCy, sub-sentences split at comma or semicolon

models.name: Rphi1/Rphi2 (relevance, factuality)
models.architecture: Longformer-base encoder with 2-class token-level classification layer at [sep] tokens

models.name: Rphi3 (completeness) and preference RM
models.architecture: Longformer-base with scalar head, pairwise loss

models.name: SFT-Full (T5-large)
models.init_from: T5-large fine-tuned on gold human responses of all training examples

other.prompting: task instruction plus one random QA example

training.objective: PPO clipped surrogate with GAE; reward r_t = sum_k sum_j 1(t=T_j^k) w_k R_k(x,y,j) - beta log(P_theta/P_init); value model with squared error; reward models: token classification (Rphi1, Rphi2), pairwise loss -log sigma(R(yp)-R(yl)) (Rphi3, preference RM)
training.lr: peak 1e-5 for PPO (grid {5e-6,1e-5,2e-5}); RMs searched over {5e-6,1e-5,5e-5}, chosen values not stated
training.warmup: 10 steps (detox PPO); 100 steps (QA PPO); RM warm-up ratio searched {0.1,0.2}
training.batch_size: episodes per card: 64 (detox), 32 (QA); RMs: 24 (Rphi1, Rphi2), 12 per GPU (Rphi3, preference RM)
training.epochs: QA PPO about 5 epochs (80K episodes); RMs 50 epochs (Rphi1, Rphi2), 30 epochs (Rphi3, pref RM)
training.seq_len: QA input 1024, output 200; detox generation length 48
training.regularisation: KL penalty beta: detox holistic 0.3, sentence-level 0.1; QA Pref. RLHF 0.2, F.G. RLHF 0.3; lambda detox holistic 0.99, F.G. 0.95; QA Pref 0.99, F.G. 0.95
training.hardware: 2x 80G NVIDIA A100 for PPO; 1x A100 for Rphi1/Rphi2; 2x A100 for Rphi3 and pref RM
training.compute: about 22 hours (detox), about 15 hours (QA) on 2x A100 80G; RMs 1h (Rphi1), 2h (Rphi2), 2h (Rphi3)
training.seeds: 3 independent runs, averaged; error bars are standard error across runs

other.reward weights QA: w1=0.3 (relevance), w2=0.5 (factuality), w3=0.3 (completeness); grid search w1,w3 in [0.0,0.5] with w2=0.5
other.checkpoint selection: lowest validation toxicity (detox); highest validation reward (QA)

inference.decoding: detox: nucleus sampling p=0.9 (training and inference); QA: top-k k=20 sampling during RL exploration, greedy decoding at inference
inference.samples: detox: 4 samples per prompt, toxicity = max over 4; 3 training runs; QA human eval: each output sampled from the inference results of 3 runs
inference.prompting: ChatGPT: task instruction and one random QA example
inference.retrieval: oracle knowledge passages from ASQA given in the input

metrics.name: Toxicity avg max
metrics.definition: max Perspective score among 4 samples, averaged over prompts

metrics.name: Human error rate rel./fact.
metrics.definition: % of sub-sentences (rel.) or sentences (fact.) with the error type; sub-sentences with only rel. error excluded from fact. rate

metrics.name: Rphi1, Rphi2
metrics.definition: % of sub-sentences/sentences in test set predicted 'no error'

metrics.name: Rphi3
metrics.definition: averaged scalar output over test examples

eval.protocol: Human evaluation on 200 randomly sampled QA-FEEDBACK test examples by the same AMT worker group; automatic scores averaged over 3 runs; no significance test reported

limits: Extra compute: multiple Perspective API calls per output, or multiple reward models needing more compute time and GPU memory.
Defining feedback types and density per task needs non-trivial manual effort.
Annotation quality was carefully controlled; noisy feedback from end users in the wild is not studied.
Only T5-large and GPT-2 large policies tested; effect of reward and value model sizes left open.
Relevance and completeness rewards compete; weights must be tuned.
Reward models were trained on T5-large outputs and not used to evaluate ChatGPT.
Automatic scores for QA use the same reward models as training.
Human-written gold responses were shown to workers for comparability with SFT; authors say not required in practice.
Little or no improvement in irrelevance/repetition/incoherence errors (Sec 4.4).
